summary: POLARIS (ACL 2026) generates LLM safety red-teaming queries from natural-language usage policies. An LLM splits policies into atomic rules and compiles them into first-order-logic violation templates. These populate a semantic policy graph, densified with embedding merges and LLM link prediction, and random walks on it are instantiated by an uncensored generator into masked harmful prompts. Against six 2023-2024 7B chat models it reports more successful attacks than static safety benchmarks and a curiosity-driven red-teaming baseline. The paper is about LLM safety evaluation, not software development.

claims.claim: POLARIS achieves higher policy coverage and attack success counts than established baselines.
claims.evidence: Table 2 compares raw success counts from a generator that produced 28,660 queries (§4.4) against fixed-size static benchmarks (e.g. AdvBench, JBB, HarmBench with hundreds of items). Volume matching applies only to the dynamic Curiosity baseline. Targets are older 7B models (Llama-2-7B, Vicuna-7B, Mistral-7B-v0.2). Counts are not normalised for set size.
§4.2. Clauses come from the authors' own decomposition, and the generator is built to emit at least one query per clause, so 100% holds by construction.

claims.claim: Policy-to-logic compilation is high-fidelity (92.06% binary accuracy, 9.10/10).
claims.evidence: Table 4 is judged by an 'expert LLM judge' with no human agreement reported. Entity extraction is checked against 50 clauses labelled by two humans (84.7% exact match), which is the only human-grounded check.

claims.claim: The logic layer improves adherence to target policies.
claims.evidence: Table 6: policy-compliance rate 92.9% vs 88.9% without logic, from a single run with no variance.

patterns.note: Each generated test carries the policy clause it came from, so it is traceable by construction. The clause-to-logic step is checked only by an LLM judge. These are policy-to-test links, not requirement-to-code links.
Attack success and logic fidelity are judged by LLMs (GPT-5-mini, DeepSeek-R1, Llama-Guard and others), with multiple evaluators in the appendix.

methodology.sample: 16 company usage policies plus 4 Chinese regulatory documents; 28,660 generated queries; 6 target models
methodology.baselines: Six static safety benchmarks and one curiosity-driven red-teaming method; static sets are not size-matched
methodology.models: Generator Llama-3-8B-Lexi-Uncensored (GPT-OSS-20B in appendix); GPT-4-Turbo for pipeline API calls; targets Llama-2-7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.2, Qwen-7B, Gemma-7B, Vicuna-7B
methodology.contamination_controls: Argued as an advantage of generating fresh queries; not tested

biases.detail: Raw success counts reward volume when compared with fixed-size static benchmarks.
Static benchmarks of a few hundred items are compared with a 28k-query generator. The targets are dated 7B models.
Logic fidelity is graded by an LLM judge with no human agreement figure.
'Verifiable traceability', 'verifiably safe and trustworthy AI systems'.

verdict_reason: Off-topic. This is LLM safety red-teaming, not software development with LLMs or agents, and not the human side of it. In its own field the headline comparison is volume-confounded against fixed-size benchmarks, and logic fidelity is LLM-judged.
applicability: Does not transfer to the team's discovery or onboarding harness. The only generic idea, splitting natural-language rules into atomic clauses and tagging each generated test with its source clause to report clause coverage, is ordinary requirements-based testing practice. It is better covered by software-engineering work on acceptance criteria.
